newsitem.title: USA: U.S. bill would require decimal stock prices.
newsitem.headline: U.S. bill would require decimal stock prices.

text.p: A bill that would require U.S. stock trades in decimals rather than fractions of $1 was introduced on Thursday by several leading members of the House of Representatives Commerce Committee.
The bill would cut the minimum spread between the bid and offer price of stocks to as little as 1 cent instead of the common one-eighth of a dollar, or 12.5 cents.

"A modern decimal system is better for small investors and better for our national competitiveness," Representative Mike Oxley, a co-sponsor of the bill, told at a news conference. He said each penny of spread costs investors over $1 billion a year.
Oxley, chairman of the Telecommunications and Finance subcommittee, promised to hold hearings on the bill in April.

Other co-sponsors include Representative Edward Markey of Massachusetts, the senior Democrat on the subcommittee, and Commerce Committee Chairman Thomas Bliley, a Virginia Republican. Securities and Exchange Commissioner Steven Wallman has also endorsed the bill.

Oxley and Markey said the United States was the only major country that does not require stock trades in decimals. They said the practice of pricing stocks in eighths of a dollar dates from the late 18th century, when an eighth of a Spanish dollar was a common currency.
